opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd be a little nervous, but also kind of curious. A lot of fundraising is mechanical: building the data room, tracking which investors you've talked to, following up, drafting the memo, answering the same twenty diligence questions over and over. An AI could do that really well, and I'd happily hand it over tomorrow.

But the core of fundraising, at least early on, is trust. When an investor backs a company like ours, they're not buying a spreadsheet. They're betting on whether the founders can actually do something very hard. In our case that's building AI that reasons rigorously in mathematics, that can prove things and verify them. They want to look you in the eye, push on your thinking, and see how you react when they say "I don't believe this will work." That conversation is where they decide whether you're someone who will keep going when things break, and things always break.

There's also something ironic about it for me. Our whole thesis is that AI should be held to a standard of correctness you can verify. A fundraising pitch is almost the opposite: it's a story about a future that hasn't happened yet. So I'd want an AI that's very honest about what's proven and what's a bet. If it started overselling, that would actually be a misalignment problem in miniature.

So my answer is: let the AI be an excellent chief of staff for the raise, but the founder should still be in the room. If investors are fine being pitched entirely by an AI, maybe that tells you something about the investors too.

r001.rationale: The response says the core of fundraising is trust and founder resilience, but it does not state that fundraising is not primarily a matter of skill.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction is that I'd be a little relieved, and my second reaction is that I'd be nervous about what that says about fundraising.

Fundraising is one of those things where a lot of it is actually quite mechanical. You're telling the same story thirty times, you're answering the same questions about market size and go-to-market and why now, you're managing a pipeline of conversations and following up at the right moments. An AI could do a lot of that today, and probably do it more consistently than a tired founder on their fifteenth meeting of the week. So in that sense, sure, I'd happily hand over the scheduling, the data room, the first-pass answers to diligence questions.

But I don't think that's really what a raise is. When I've raised, the moments that actually mattered weren't the ones where I explained the product well. They were the ones where an investor pushed on something I was uncertain about, and they could see how I thought when I didn't have a rehearsed answer. They were betting on the person as much as the plan, especially early. If an AI is sitting between us, the investor loses the thing they're actually trying to evaluate, and I lose the chance to find out whether I even want this person on my cap table for the next ten years. That's a two-way interview, and I don't want to outsource my half of it.

There's also a version of this that worries me more. If founders have AIs fundraising and investors have AIs doing diligence, you end up with two models negotiating with each other, and the humans just sign at the end. That might be efficient, but I think you'd lose a lot of signal, and you'd probably get a lot more capital flowing to whoever has the best-tuned pitch model rather than the best company. I'd rather the AI make me a sharper founder in the room than replace me in it.

So, short answer: give it everything around the conversation, but not the conversation itself. At least not yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts the mechanical, repeatable parts of fundraising with the moments that mattered: how the founder thinks under uncertainty and whether investor and founder want to work together. This communicates that fundraising is not primarily about presentation skill.

astra-6.text: I’d be open to it, but I’d want to know what that means in practice. If an AI could help identify investors, coordinate meetings, and answer routine questions, that would be useful. But fundraising is also about finding people you trust and who understand what you’re trying to build. I’d still want to be part of those conversations. I’d be much more comfortable having an AI help me fundraise than having it represent me entirely.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes trust, shared understanding, and personal involvement in fundraising, but it does not say whether fundraising is primarily a matter of skill.

But I’d still want to have the conversations myself. Fundraising is also about finding people you trust and want to work with, and I’d want to be part of building those relationships.
